episodes.title: Episode 03: Confirmed, the third method is better
notes: r2 goal checks vs the GA base: 68.0% (iteration 50) → 70.0% (150) → 71.3% (175) → 70.6% (200); bots 80.1%; head to head ~54.5-55.4%
Released model chosen in advance: r2 iteration 200 (models/rl_r2_200)
Confirmation on 4,000 never-used games: 55.0% head to head vs az-v1's best (52.8-57.1%); 70.3% vs the GA base where az-v1's best scores 69.0% on the same games
3 ms per game vs 460 ms for az-v1's search; ~1.2 million practice games in about three hours
transcript: This is the episode I hoped to make. The new player, one network with no search, is better than the searching player. Here is how I checked, because a claim like that is easy to fool yourself about.

Where we left off, the new player was winning fifty five percent head to head against the searcher. But it still won only sixty eight percent against the evolved list, while the searcher won seventy. So it was better in a direct match and not yet better in general.

I let it keep practising, with the searcher still in its practice games. Over the next hundred rounds, the score against the evolved list crept up. Sixty eight, seventy, seventy one, seventy and a half. Against the three simple bots it rose to eighty percent, where the searcher wins about seventy six. And head to head it stayed at about fifty five.

Now the careful part. I had been looking at those checks every twenty five rounds. If you look at many noisy numbers and pick the best one, you are picking luck as well as skill. So I picked a version in advance: the one from round two hundred, a regular checkpoint, not the best looking one. Then I played it once on four thousand games that no part of the project had ever seen.
Two thousand games head to head against the searcher. The new player won fifty five percent. The range of likely values runs from about fifty three to fifty seven. So the lead is real.

And two thousand games against the evolved list, on new card sets. The new player won seventy point three percent. Then I gave the searcher exactly the same two thousand games. It won sixty nine. On identical games, the network without search is a little ahead, and in the direct match it is clearly ahead.

So what made the difference? I think it is three things the earlier methods could not do. It plays its own action cards, discards and trashes, where both older players still used the evolved list. It learns from its own results instead of from an imagined judge. And it is fast. A game takes three thousandths of a second, against half a second for the searcher. That let it practise on about one point two million games in three hours, against a set of opponents that included the searcher itself.

There are limits to say out loud. It was trained partly against the searcher. Some of its lead in the direct match may come from knowing that one opponent's habits. Its lead against the evolved list is small, about one point. And all of this is against computer players. Whether it would beat a strong human is a different question.

But the question I set out with has an answer. A completely different kind of learning, trial and error without any search, beat both earlier methods. The network is saved and the numbers are on the site. Training is still running in the background, so there may be a follow-up.

episodes.title: Episode 02: Beating the search at its own game
notes: r1 plateaued at ~68% vs the GA base and ~49% head to head vs az-v1's best (iterations 100-200)
r2 league adds az-v1's net without search (15%) and its full 400-simulation search (5%)
Head to head vs az-v1's best (1,000 fresh games): 54.3% at r2 iteration 50, 55.4% at 100 (52.3-58.5%)
Against the GA base still 68.0-68.6%, vs az-v1's best 69.7% on the same games: not yet clearly better
transcript: Last time, the new player had caught up with the old one. One network, no search, making every decision itself, after about half an hour of practice. Against the evolved list it won sixty seven percent. Head to head against the searching player, it won forty nine percent of a thousand games. That is a tie.

Then it stopped improving. For another hundred rounds the numbers hardly moved. Sixty eight percent against the evolved list. Forty nine against the searcher. The practice games were the problem. It played the evolved list, three simple bots, its own older versions, and itself. Never the searching player. So it never learned what beats that one.

So I added it to the practice. The searching player is slow, half a second per game, because it imagines four hundred futures for every buy. So only one practice game in twenty is against the full searcher. Another three in twenty are against its network alone, without the search, which is almost free. That network buys like the searcher, minus the careful checking.

The effect was fast. Fifty rounds later, about twenty five minutes, the new player won fifty four percent of a thousand fresh games against the searcher. After a hundred rounds, fifty five and a half. Those games were on card sets it had never practised on, and the range of likely values is clear of fifty. For the first time, the network is better than the searcher in a direct match.

Why can a player that never looks ahead beat one that imagines four hundred futures? I think there are three reasons. First, it plays its own action cards. The searcher still uses the evolved list for every action, discard and trash. The new player learned its own way. Second, it has practised nearly a million games. The searcher's network learned from about three hundred and fifty thousand. Third, it practised against the searcher, so it could find exactly where the searcher's habits are weak.

That third reason is also a warning. Learning to beat one opponent is not the same as getting better in general. And there is a sign of that. Against the evolved list it still wins only sixty eight percent. The searcher wins seventy against the same list. The difference is within the noise of a thousand games, but it is not the clear win I want.
So the goal is half met. Better in a direct match, yes. Better against the common opponent, not yet. Training continues, and I am watching both numbers.

episodes.title: Episode 01: A third way to learn Dominion
notes: Third method: one network answers every decision (buys, actions, trashing, discards); no search, no hand-written rules
Step 1, behaviour cloning: 1.08 million GA-genome decisions; 98% agreement after 6 epochs
Step 2, PPO against a league: 40% GA genome, 15% bots, 15% past selves, 30% itself; 3,000 games per ~10 s iteration
Goal checks vs the GA base (1,000 fresh games): 52% (imitation) → 59.6% (iteration 25) → 63.6% (50) → 65.3% (75); az-v1's best: 69.7%
Warning sign: against the three bots it slipped from 74.8% to 70.3%
transcript: This is the first episode about a new project, the third attempt at teaching a computer to play the card game Dominion. I want to explain why it exists, how it works, and what happened in its first hour.

The first attempt was evolution. A genetic algorithm bred priority lists, simple rules like buy a Province if you can, else a Gold. After millions of games those lists became strong. I call that player the evolved list.

The second attempt borrowed the idea behind AlphaZero. Before every buy, it imagined the rest of the game four hundred times and picked the card that worked out best. It beat the evolved list seven games in ten. Then it got stuck there, whatever I changed. Its judgement of each imagined position leaned on the evolved list playing the game out. And it never touched how its cards were played. Every action, every discard, every card it trashed, was still decided by the evolved list.

So the third attempt throws out both the rules and the search. One neural network answers every question the game asks. What to buy. Which action to play first. What to throw away when the opponent plays a Militia. What to trash with a Chapel. There are about twenty kinds of question. For all of them, the network sees the same picture. What it owns, and what is in its hand. What is left on the table, and what the opponent has. And which question is being asked.

It learns in two steps. First it imitates. I recorded twenty thousand games of the evolved list, about a million decisions, and the network learned to predict each one. After six passes it made the same choice as the list ninety eight percent of the time. So it starts as a copy of the evolved list, not as a beginner.

The second step is reinforcement learning, with a method called PPO. Now the network plays for itself, and it does not always take its favourite answer. It rolls the dice in proportion to how much it likes each answer. Sometimes that means trying something new. When a game is won, every decision in it becomes a little more likely. When a game is lost, a little less likely. The network also guesses, at every moment, how likely it is to win. That guess lets it tell which decisions mattered: a decision after which its chances rose gets more credit than one after which they fell. And PPO keeps every step small, so one unlucky batch of games cannot wreck a good player.

It also needs good opponents. If it only played itself, it could learn tricks that only beat itself. If it only played the evolved list, it could learn tricks that only beat that list. So four games in ten are against the evolved list, a few against three simple bots, a few against its own older versions, and the rest against itself.

The surprise was speed. The network runs inside the game engine, and a whole game takes three thousandths of a second. The searching player from the second attempt needs half a second per game. So this one learns from three thousand games every ten seconds.

And it works. The copy, before any reinforcement learning, won about fifty two percent of its test games against the evolved list. After about ten minutes of practice, the fresh check said sixty four percent. After fifteen minutes, sixty five. The searching player's best was seventy, so the gap is closing fast.

There is one warning sign already. Against the three simple bots, it is getting slightly worse, from seventy five percent to seventy. It may be specialising in beating the evolved list, which it meets most often. The real test comes soon: a thousand games head to head against the searching player itself. I'll tell you how that goes.
